# Summary: A 1997 UK General Election Manifesto

This manifesto presented a vision of national renewal focused on modernising Britain across multiple policy areas while maintaining economic stability.

## Economic Policy
The document committed to fiscal responsibility, promising to work within existing spending allocations for two years and maintain low inflation targets. It pledged no increases to basic or top income tax rates, with a long-term goal of introducing a ten pence starting rate. A windfall levy on privatised utilities would fund employment programmes. The approach emphasised efficient spending over increased expenditure, with investment priorities in education, infrastructure, and skills development.

## Education
Education was designated the primary policy focus. Key commitments included reducing class sizes for young children, guaranteeing nursery places for four-year-olds, and establishing literacy and numeracy standards. The manifesto proposed modernising comprehensive education through ability-based setting within schools, creating a "University for Industry" for lifelong learning, and connecting schools to information technology networks. Failing schools would face intervention or closure with "fresh starts."

## Healthcare
The manifesto proposed reforming internal market structures within the health service to reduce administrative costs, redirecting savings toward patient care. It committed to real-terms spending increases annually, reducing waiting lists, establishing a food standards agency, and appointing a public health minister to address underlying causes of illness.

## Crime and Justice
A "tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime" approach combined personal responsibility with addressing social factors. Specific proposals included faster processing of youth offenders, prosecution service reforms, community safety orders, racial harassment legislation, and an anti-drugs coordinator. The document supported stricter firearms controls.

## Welfare and Employment
The centrepiece welfare-to-work programme aimed to move 250,000 young unemployed people into jobs through four pathways: subsidised private sector employment, voluntary sector work, full-time education, or environmental taskforce positions. Long-term unemployed adults would receive similar support. Lone parents would receive employment assistance once children entered school.

## Family and Housing
Policies supported work-family balance through childcare strategies and limits on working hours. Housing measures included releasing council house sale receipts for new construction, protections for homeowners against gazumping, licensing for multiple-occupancy properties, and stronger homelessness duties. Pension policy retained the basic state pension while promoting "stakeholder pensions" and reviewing long-term care funding.

## Constitutional Reform
Significant democratic changes included removing hereditary peers' voting rights, establishing devolved parliaments for Scotland and Wales (subject to referendums), creating an elected London authority with a mayor, incorporating human rights conventions into domestic law, and introducing freedom of information legislation. Regional development agencies would coordinate economic planning in England.

## Europe and International Affairs
The manifesto advocated active engagement in European institutions rather than withdrawal or marginalisation, supporting single market completion, institutional reform, and enlargement eastward. It maintained three conditions for potential single currency membership: cabinet agreement, parliamentary approval, and public referendum. Defence policy retained nuclear deterrent capability while supporting multilateral disarmament negotiations and stronger arms export controls. International development would receive renewed focus with a dedicated cabinet minister.

## Environment and Transport
Environmental considerations would inform all government departments, supported by parliamentary audit mechanisms. Transport policy emphasised integration across modes, with strategic railway oversight, public-private partnerships for London Underground, and promotion of cleaner vehicles. The document opposed new nuclear power stations while supporting renewable energy development.
